overview: Ramappa Temple, officially the Kakatiya Rudreshwara (Ramappa) Temple, is a magnificent 13th-century Shiva temple at Palampet village, Venkatapur Mandal, Mulugu District, Telangana. Constructed between 1212 and 1234 CE (construction began 1213 CE), it is the main Shiva temple in a walled complex built during the Kakatiya period under rulers Rudradeva and Recharla Rudra, and is rare among Indian temples in being named after its chief sculptor, Ramappa. Built of red sandstone, carved granite and dolerite, with a distinctive pyramidal Vimana (stepped tower) made of lightweight porous 'floating bricks' that reduce the roof's weight, it is celebrated for its intricate carvings, the 'Salabhanjikas / Madanika' bracket figures, and the 6-foot-high star-shaped platform. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site on 25 July 2021 (reference 1570, India's 39th WHS, 44th session), it is geographically and administratively separate from the Thousand Pillar Temple at Hanamakonda (~75 km away).
summary: Ramappa Temple (Kakatiya Rudreshwara Temple) at Palampet, Mulugu District, Telangana, is a 13th-century Kakatiya Shiva temple and a UNESCO World Heritage Site (inscribed 25 July 2021, ref 1570). Construction began in 1213 CE under Kakatiya king Ganapati Deva, commissioned by his general Recharla Rudra, and is named after its sculptor Ramappa. Built of red sandstone, granite, dolerite and lightweight 'floating bricks' on a star-shaped platform, it has survived multiple earthquakes thanks to advanced Kakatiya engineering. It is the ACTUAL UNESCO World Heritage Site — not the Thousand Pillar Temple at Hanamakonda (~75 km away), which is only on UNESCO's tentative list. The temple is surrounded by the Ramappa Cheruvu (Kakatiya-built reservoir) and is celebrated for the 'Salabhanjikas' dancing-girl bracket figures.

history.content: The Ramappa Temple complex was constructed between 1212 and 1234 CE (construction began 1213 CE) during the reign of the Kakatiya king Ganapati Deva. It was commissioned by his military commander Recharla Rudra (also rendered Recharla Rudra Reddy). The temple is unusual in being named after its chief sculptor/architect, Ramappa, rather than its presiding deity (the deity is Ramalingeshwara Swamy, a form of Shiva). Marco Polo, during his visit to the Kakatiya empire, supposedly called the temple 'the brightest star in the galaxy of temples'. The temple faces east and is approached by a long flight of stairs from the east, north and south. The cornice above the three gateways is supported by black basalt brackets in the shape of dancing girls (Salabhanjikas) — four per gate, totalling 12 — with the remaining brackets representing yallis (mythical lion-elephant hybrids).
founders: Kakatiya King Ganapati Deva (reigning patron, r. 1199–1262)
legends: Marco Polo, on visiting the Kakatiya empire, reportedly called the temple 'the brightest star in the galaxy of (medieval Deccan) temples'.

history.content: Despite surviving several earthquakes over the centuries, the temple remains remarkably well preserved due to its advanced engineering techniques (sandbox foundation and lightweight 'floating brick' Vimana). Academic research on the temple's engineering began in the 1980s under Prof. M. Panduranga Rao. In 1931 CE, Ghulam Yazdani published 'The Temples at Palampet' (Memoirs of the ASI, No. 6), one of the earliest systematic studies. On 25 July 2021, at the 44th session of the UNESCO World Heritage Committee, the Kakatiya Rudreshwara (Ramappa) Temple was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site (cultural criteria i and iii, reference 1570) — India's 39th World Heritage Site and the first such site in Telangana. The temple is centrally protected and maintained by the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) under the AMASR Act, 2010; the buffer zone extends 300 m from the core zone boundary.

sthala_puranam: The presiding deity is Lord Ramalingeshwara Swamy (a form of Lord Shiva). The temple's popular lore is largely tied to the historical patronage of the Kakatiya rulers and the legend of the chief sculptor Ramappa, after whom the temple is named — making it one of the rare Indian temples named after its architect rather than its presiding deity. A separate, less-verified sasthala tradition is that the Sasan Mandap houses a Sanskrit inscription of 'Rudra-senapati' from the Kakatiya era.
religious_significance: Ramappa Temple is an important Shaivite pilgrimage destination in Telangana. Devotees visit to seek the blessings of Lord Shiva (as Ramalingeshwara Swamy) for prosperity, health and spiritual well-being. Beyond its religious role, it is regarded as one of India's greatest architectural achievements, admired by scholars and visitors worldwide.
spiritual_significance: An important Shaivite pilgrimage site dedicated to Lord Ramalingeshwara (Shiva), where devotees seek prosperity, health and spiritual well-being, while also revering the temple as a pinnacle of Kakatiya artistry and faith. The temple complex's setting — at the foothills of a forested area and amidst agricultural fields, close to the shores of the Ramappa Cheruvu (a Kakatiya-built reservoir) — follows the ideology and practice sanctioned in dharmic texts that temples are to be constructed to form an integral part of a natural setting (hills, forests, springs, streams, lakes, catchment areas, and agricultural lands).
healing_beliefs: Blessings of prosperity, health and spiritual well-being through worship of Lord Shiva (Ramalingeshwara Swamy)
miracles_and_devotee_experiences: The temple has survived multiple earthquakes over the centuries with remarkable preservation, widely attributed to its advanced Kakatiya engineering (sandbox foundation and lightweight 'floating brick' Vimana).

The 'floating bricks' used in the Vimana (shikhara) are reportedly so porous and lightweight that they float in water, per multiple sources (a popular claim that is widely repeated in tourism/heritage literature).
Devotees and visitors describe a serene, spiritually charged atmosphere in the walled complex.
architecture: Ramappa Temple is built in the Kakatiya architectural style (Kakatiya, Bhumija / Vesara), using red sandstone, black basalt, carved granite and dolerite, with a distinctive pyramidal Vimana (horizontally stepped tower) made of lightweight porous 'floating bricks' that reduce the weight of the roof structures. The central shrine has a star-shaped plan and stands on a 6-foot-high plinth. The temple faces east and is approached by a long flight of stairs from east, north and south. The cornice above the three gateways is supported by black basalt brackets in the shape of dancing girls (Salabhanjikas) — four per gate, totalling 12 — with the remaining brackets representing yallis (mythical lion-elephant hybrids). The interior houses a Shiva Linga in the inner sanctum, entered through an ornamental gateway of shining black basalt. Basalt pillars with intricate ornamentation support the roof of the open space in front of the inner sanctum. The exterior walls have rich relief ornamentations. The complex includes the main Rudreshwara shrine, a Nandi Mandap (east of the main shrine — the beautifully decorated mandap roof has collapsed, but the Nandi statue remains in full glory under the open sky), a Gaurishia / Gouri Temple (north, smaller, same plan, spire collapsed), an Asthana Mandap (south, in ruins), and a Sasan Mandap (housing a Sanskrit pillar inscription of Rudra-senapati from the Kakatiya era).

As a protected heritage monument managed by ASI, the complex is largely free to enter (most sources: 'Non ticketed / Free', updated Mar 2025 on WikiVoyage); visitors should check current ASI regulations for any monument-related entry charges.

best_time_to_visit: October to March for pleasant weather. Visit early morning for a peaceful experience; carry drinking water during summer and wear comfortable footwear while exploring the complex. top_reviews: The Ramappa Temple, located in Palampet village, Telangana, is a 13th-century UNESCO World Heritage Site dedicated to Lord Shiva. Built between 1213 and 1323 CE, it is renowned for its sandbox foundation, intricate basalt carvings, and lightweight 'floating bricks' used in the spire. It is a premier example of Kakatiya architecture. Inscribed in 2021 as a World Heritage Site, it is the first such site in Telangana. Situated in Palampet, Mulugu district, approximately 200 km from Hyderabad and 66 km from Warangal. Built in 1213 CE by Recherla Rudra, a general of the Kakatiya king Ganapathi Deva, and designed by the sculptor Ramappa. The temple rests on a 'sand-box' foundation, which provides stability during earthquakes. The shikhara (tower) is built with lightweight, porous bricks that float in water. It features intricate carvings on black basalt stone, depicting scenes from Hindu mythology and dance, often referred to as the 'crest jewel' of Kakatiya art. The temple is open to visitors from 6 AM to 6 PM. The temple is also known as the Rudreshwara Temple. Visitors are often advised to take personal transport from Mulugu, as public transport options to Palampet are limited.

introduction.en: Ramappa Temple, officially the Kakatiya Rudreshwara Temple, is a 13th-century Shiva temple at Palampet in Mulugu district, Telangana, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 25 July 2021. Construction began in 1213 CE under Kakatiya king Ganapati Deva, commissioned by his general Recharla Rudra, and the temple is named after its sculptor Ramappa. It is celebrated for its red sandstone and dolerite carvings, the 12 Salabhanjika dancing-girl bracket figures, the 6-foot-high star-shaped platform, and the distinctive pyramidal Vimana of lightweight porous floating bricks. It is a separate monument from the Thousand Pillar Temple at Hanamakonda.

history.en: Construction of the Ramappa Temple complex began in 1213 CE during the reign of Kakatiya king Ganapati Deva, commissioned by his general Recharla Rudra, and continued for about 40 years. It is named after its chief sculptor, Ramappa — unusual for an Indian temple. Marco Polo, on visiting the Kakatiya empire, reportedly called it the brightest star in the galaxy of medieval Deccan temples. Despite surviving several earthquakes, the temple remains remarkably preserved thanks to its sandbox foundation and floating-brick Vimana. On 25 July 2021, UNESCO inscribed it as World Heritage Site reference 1570, India's 39th such site and the first in Telangana.

travel_guide.en: Ramappa Temple is in Palampet village, Venkatapur Mandal, Mulugu district, Telangana, about 200 to 209 kilometres from Hyderabad and 66 kilometres from Warangal. It is well connected by road via NH 505 (Warangal–Mulugu route) using TSRTC buses, taxis and private vehicles. The nearest railway station is Warangal, about 66 kilometres away; the nearest airport is Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Hyderabad, about 200 to 210 kilometres. The temple is open daily from 6:00 AM to 6:00 PM, with an evening Sound & Light Show at 7:00 PM. October to March is the best season.

faq.question: What are the temple timings?
faq.answer: The temple is open daily from 6:00 AM to 6:00 PM (morning session 6:00 AM–12:00 PM, afternoon session 12:00 PM–6:00 PM). An evening Sound & Light Show is held at 7:00 PM (Telugu / English) on a separate ticket — confirm availability locally.

faq.question: Is there any entry fee?
faq.answer: General entry for worship is free (most sources, including WikiVoyage 'Non ticketed (Free), updated Mar 2025'). As an ASI-protected monument, visitors should check current ASI regulations for any monument-related entry charges.

faq.question: Why is Ramappa Temple famous?
faq.answer: It is famous for its Kakatiya architecture, the 12 Salabhanjika (dancing-girl) bracket figures, the 6-foot-high star-shaped platform, the lightweight 'floating brick' Vimana, the sandbox foundation engineering, and its UNESCO World Heritage status (inscribed 25 July 2021, ref 1570).

faq.question: Who built Ramappa Temple?
faq.answer: It was commissioned in 1213 CE by the military commander Recharla Rudra (also rendered Recharla Rudra Reddy) during the reign of Kakatiya King Ganapati Deva (r. 1199–1262), and named after its chief sculptor/architect Ramappa. Construction continued for about 40 years (c. 1212–1234 CE).

faq.question: Which deity is worshipped here?
faq.answer: Lord Ramalingeshwara Swamy (Lord Shiva) is the presiding deity, represented by a Shiva Linga in the inner sanctum.

faq.question: When was Ramappa Temple inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
faq.answer: It was inscribed on 25 July 2021 at the 44th session of the UNESCO World Heritage Committee, as reference 1570 under cultural criteria (i) and (iii). It is India's 39th World Heritage Site and the first in Telangana.

faq.question: Is the Ramappa Temple the same as the Thousand Pillar Temple?
faq.answer: No. They are two distinct Kakatiya monuments. The Ramappa Temple is in Palampet, Mulugu District (~200 km NE of Hyderabad, ~66 km from Warangal), is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2021), was built 1213 CE under Ganapati Deva by Recharla Rudra, and is dedicated to Shiva (Ramalingeshwara). The Thousand Pillar Temple is in Hanamakonda, Hanamakonda District (~150 km from Hyderabad), is only on UNESCO's tentative list, was built 1163 CE under Rudra Deva, and is a Trikutalayam of Shiva, Vishnu and Surya. They are about 75 km apart.

faq.question: Which festivals are celebrated?
faq.answer: Major festivals include Maha Shivaratri, Karthika Masam, Ugadi, Sankranti, Deepavali and Pradosham celebrations.

faq.question: Is photography allowed?
faq.answer: Photography is generally allowed in the temple's exterior areas, subject to ASI rules. No flash inside the sanctum. Respect any restrictions inside protected sections.

faq.question: Is parking available?
faq.answer: Yes. Parking facilities are available near the temple complex.

faq.question: What are the nearby attractions?
faq.answer: Ramappa Lake (Kakatiya-built reservoir, immediately adjacent), Kota Gullu (Ghanpur) group of 22 temples (~9 km), Laknavaram Lake, Thousand Pillar Temple at Hanamakonda (~75 km), Bhadrakali Temple, Warangal Fort, Pakhal Lake, Eturnagaram Wildlife Sanctuary, and Pochampalli Village (famous for ikat handlooms).

faq.question: Why is Ramappa Temple a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
faq.answer: It received UNESCO World Heritage status on 25 July 2021 (ref 1570) because of its exceptional Kakatiya architecture (cultural criteria i and iii), innovative engineering techniques such as the sandbox foundation and the lightweight 'floating brick' Vimana, the 12 Salabhanjika bracket figures, the temple's harmonious natural setting near Ramappa Lake, and its outstanding cultural and historical significance. It is the first UNESCO World Heritage Site in Telangana.
